proteins.name: Myoglobin
proteins.tagline: The first protein whose 3-D structure was ever solved.
proteins.description: Myoglobin stores and releases oxygen inside muscle cells, and it gives red meat its colour. In 1958 John Kendrew used X-ray crystallography to solve its structure, producing the first three-dimensional atomic model of any protein. Its single globin chain cradles an iron-bearing heme group that binds one molecule of oxygen.
proteins.fun_fact: Diving mammals such as whales and seals pack their muscles with so much myoglobin that the tissue looks almost black.

proteins.name: Hemoglobin
proteins.tagline: The oxygen ferry of your blood.
proteins.description: Hemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and helps ferry carbon dioxide back again. Each molecule is a tetramer of four globin chains, each holding a heme group, and the four subunits cooperate so that binding one oxygen makes the next bind more easily. Max Perutz spent over two decades solving its structure, sharing the 1962 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Kendrew.
proteins.fun_fact: A single red blood cell carries roughly 270 million hemoglobin molecules.

proteins.name: Lysozyme
proteins.tagline: A natural antibiotic in your tears and saliva.
proteins.description: Lysozyme defends against bacteria by chopping up the sugar chains of their cell walls, and it is found in tears, saliva, mucus and egg white. In 1965 David Phillips determined its structure, the first enzyme ever visualised in three dimensions, revealing a cleft that grips and cleaves its target. Alexander Fleming discovered lysozyme years before he discovered penicillin.
proteins.fun_fact: Fleming reportedly discovered lysozyme after a drop from his own runny nose landed on a bacterial culture and cleared a patch of it.

proteins.name: Green Fluorescent Protein
proteins.tagline: The glowing lantern that lets scientists watch life happen.
proteins.description: Green fluorescent protein glows bright green under blue or ultraviolet light, forming its own chromophore from three of its own amino acids without any external cofactor. Cloned from a Pacific jellyfish, it became a revolutionary biological beacon that lets scientists watch genes switch on and proteins move inside living cells. Its discovery and development won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
proteins.fun_fact: GFP's barrel shape is often called a 'beta-can': eleven strands wrapped around the glowing core like staves around a barrel.

proteins.name: Insulin
proteins.tagline: The hormone that keeps your blood sugar in check.
proteins.description: Insulin signals cells to take up glucose from the blood, and its absence or malfunction causes diabetes. It is a small protein of two chains stitched together by disulfide bonds. Insulin was the first protein to be fully sequenced, by Frederick Sanger, and among the first to have its structure solved, by Dorothy Hodgkin, each achievement recognised with a Nobel Prize.
proteins.fun_fact: Insulin was the first human protein manufactured with recombinant DNA, produced in 1978.

proteins.name: Ubiquitin
proteins.tagline: The molecular tag that marks proteins for the scrapheap.
proteins.description: Ubiquitin is a tiny 76-amino-acid tag that cells attach to other proteins to label them, most famously for destruction by the proteasome. This labelling system controls protein turnover, DNA repair and cell signalling, and its discovery earned the 2004 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Ubiquitin is one of the most highly conserved proteins known, nearly identical from yeast to humans.
proteins.fun_fact: Its name comes from 'ubiquitous', because it is found in virtually every tissue of every complex cell.

proteins.name: Cytochrome c
proteins.tagline: An ancient electron courier with a deadly second job.
proteins.description: Cytochrome c is a small heme protein that shuttles electrons along the respiratory chain in mitochondria, a key step in making cellular energy. When a cell decides to die, cytochrome c leaks out of the mitochondria and helps trigger apoptosis, giving it a dramatic double life. Because it is so ancient and conserved, its sequence is a classic molecular clock for tracing evolution.
proteins.fun_fact: Human and chimpanzee cytochrome c are identical; humans differ from horses by only about a dozen amino acids.

proteins.name: Ribonuclease A
proteins.tagline: The enzyme that taught us how proteins fold.
proteins.description: Ribonuclease A cuts RNA and became a workhorse of early molecular biology. Christian Anfinsen showed that this enzyme, once unfolded, could refold on its own into its correct shape, proving that a protein's amino-acid sequence carries all the information needed to fold it, an insight recognised with the 1972 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. It was also one of the first enzymes to be chemically synthesised from scratch.
proteins.fun_fact: Work on ribonuclease A contributed to several different Nobel Prizes over the decades.

proteins.name: Carbonic Anhydrase II
proteins.tagline: One of the fastest enzymes in your body.
proteins.description: Carbonic anhydrase speeds up the interconversion of carbon dioxide and bicarbonate, a reaction essential for transporting CO2 in the blood and balancing pH. It is one of the fastest enzymes known, converting up to a million molecules per second with the help of a single zinc ion. It is a drug target for glaucoma, altitude sickness and epilepsy.
proteins.fun_fact: Without this enzyme, your blood could not clear carbon dioxide fast enough to keep up with your breathing.

proteins.name: p53 Tumour Suppressor
proteins.tagline: The 'guardian of the genome'.
proteins.description: p53 senses DNA damage and can halt cell division or trigger cell death, stopping damaged cells from turning cancerous. Its gene is the single most frequently mutated gene in human cancers, disabled in roughly half of all tumours. This structure shows its core domain gripping DNA, exactly where many cancer-causing mutations strike.
proteins.fun_fact: Elephants carry around twenty copies of the p53 gene, which may help explain why they rarely get cancer.

proteins.name: Rhodopsin
proteins.tagline: The light switch that lets you see in the dark.
proteins.description: Rhodopsin is the light-sensing pigment in the rod cells of the eye that enables vision in dim light. A single photon can twist its embedded retinal molecule and fire off a signalling cascade. As the first G-protein-coupled receptor to have its structure solved, it became a template for understanding an enormous family of drug-target receptors.
proteins.fun_fact: About a third of all modern medicines act on GPCRs, the receptor family that rhodopsin represents.

proteins.name: Bacteriorhodopsin
proteins.tagline: A solar-powered proton pump from salt-loving microbes.
proteins.description: Bacteriorhodopsin uses sunlight to push protons across a membrane, storing energy for the cell. Its seven membrane-spanning helices made it a classic model for how membrane proteins are built and how they work. It colours patches of microbial membranes a vivid purple.
proteins.fun_fact: Its 'purple membrane' has even inspired ideas for light-powered biological computer memory.

proteins.name: KcsA Potassium Channel
proteins.tagline: The channel that revealed how cells choose their ions.
proteins.description: KcsA is a potassium channel that showed how cells let potassium ions through a membrane while turning away the smaller sodium ion. Roderick MacKinnon's structure revealed a 'selectivity filter' that mimics the watery shell potassium prefers, work that won the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Channels like this underlie every nerve impulse and heartbeat.
proteins.fun_fact: The channel is fussier than a bouncer: it waves through the larger potassium ion and rejects the smaller sodium one.

proteins.name: Aquaporin
proteins.tagline: The molecular water pipe in your cells.
proteins.description: Aquaporins are channels that let water rush across cell membranes while blocking ions and even protons, keeping cells, kidneys and eyes properly hydrated. Their discovery solved the long-standing puzzle of how water crosses membranes so quickly, earning a share of the 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A clever electrostatic trick in the pore stops protons from leaking through.
proteins.fun_fact: Your kidneys rely on aquaporins to reabsorb around 150 litres of water every single day.

proteins.name: RuBisCO
proteins.tagline: Probably the most abundant protein on Earth.
proteins.description: RuBisCO captures carbon dioxide from the air and fixes it into sugar during photosynthesis, the gateway for nearly all carbon entering the living world. It is thought to be the most abundant protein on the planet. It is also famously slow, and it sometimes grabs oxygen by mistake, a quirk that plants must constantly work around.
proteins.fun_fact: There may be more RuBisCO on Earth than any other protein, on the order of a thousand kilograms for every living person.

proteins.name: Ferritin
proteins.tagline: Your body's iron warehouse.
proteins.description: Ferritin is a hollow protein sphere built from 24 subunits that can lock away thousands of iron atoms and release them when needed. By keeping iron safely stored, it prevents the loose metal from generating damaging free radicals. A blood ferritin test is a common way doctors check your iron stores.
proteins.fun_fact: One ferritin shell can hold up to about 4,500 iron atoms inside its nano-sized cage.

proteins.name: GroEL / GroES Chaperonin
proteins.tagline: A protein-folding chamber powered by ATP.
proteins.description: GroEL gives newly made proteins a private, protected space to fold correctly, capped by its partner GroES. Powered by ATP, it repeatedly encloses and releases its client proteins until they reach the right shape. Chaperones like this keep cells from filling up with tangled, misfolded proteins.
proteins.fun_fact: Its double-ringed barrel acts like a tiny sheltered room where a protein can fold away from the crowded, sticky interior of the cell.

proteins.name: Trypsin
proteins.tagline: A molecular scalpel from your gut.
proteins.description: Trypsin is a digestive enzyme that cuts dietary proteins into smaller pieces in the small intestine. It is a serine protease, using a precisely arranged trio of amino acids to snip protein chains at specific spots. Biochemists prize it as a molecular scalpel for cutting proteins at predictable positions.
proteins.fun_fact: Trypsin only cuts after the amino acids lysine or arginine, making its cuts neat and predictable, a gift to protein chemists.

proteins.name: Chymotrypsin
proteins.tagline: The textbook example of how enzymes work.
proteins.description: Chymotrypsin is a digestive serine protease that works alongside trypsin to break down the proteins you eat. It became a classic example for understanding how enzymes accelerate reactions using a 'catalytic triad' of amino acids. Its mechanism helped define how an entire family of enzymes operates.
proteins.fun_fact: It is choosy in a different way from trypsin, cutting next to bulky, oily amino acids like phenylalanine and tryptophan.

proteins.name: Actin
proteins.tagline: The filament that lets your cells move and your muscles pull.
proteins.description: Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in our cells, forming filaments that give cells their shape, let them crawl, and provide the tracks that muscles pull against. Its building blocks snap together into long, dynamic filaments that constantly grow and shrink. Together with myosin, actin powers every muscle contraction.
proteins.fun_fact: Every time a muscle moves, it is a molecular tug-of-war between actin filaments and myosin motors.

proteins.name: Tubulin
proteins.tagline: The scaffolding and railway of your cells.
proteins.description: Tubulin assembles into microtubules, stiff hollow tubes that act as the cell's scaffolding and railways, and that pull chromosomes apart when a cell divides. Because dividing cancer cells depend on microtubules, tubulin is the target of important chemotherapy drugs such as taxol. This structure was solved with a special method using flattened protein sheets and electrons rather than crystals.
proteins.fun_fact: Cancer drugs like taxol work by freezing microtubules so that dividing cells cannot separate their chromosomes.

proteins.name: HIV-1 Protease
proteins.tagline: A drug-design triumph against AIDS.
proteins.description: HIV protease is the molecular scissors the AIDS virus needs to cut its proteins into working parts; block it and the virus cannot mature. It became one of the great success stories of structure-based drug design, guiding the protease-inhibitor drugs that transformed HIV into a manageable condition. It is a small but mighty enzyme built from two identical halves.
proteins.fun_fact: Protease inhibitors designed against structures like this helped turn an HIV diagnosis from a death sentence into a treatable illness.

proteins.name: Immunoglobulin G (Antibody)
proteins.tagline: The Y-shaped workhorse of your immune system.
proteins.description: Immunoglobulin G is the classic Y-shaped antibody, the workhorse of immune defence that recognises and tags invaders for destruction. Its two arm-tips can be tailored to grip almost any target, while its stem recruits the rest of the immune system. Antibodies like these are now engineered into a huge class of modern medicines.
proteins.fun_fact: IgG is the only antibody that crosses the placenta, giving newborns their mother's immunity for their first months of life.

proteins.name: Collagen
proteins.tagline: The most abundant protein in your body.
proteins.description: Collagen is the body's main structural protein, the tough cabling in skin, tendon, bone and cartilage, and the most abundant protein in mammals. Three chains wind around each other into a rope-like triple helix, giving tissues their tensile strength. This model peptide let scientists see that triple helix at atomic detail.
proteins.fun_fact: Collagen makes up roughly a third of all the protein in your body.

proteins.name: ATP Synthase (F1)
proteins.tagline: The rotary engine that makes your energy currency.
proteins.description: ATP synthase is a rotary engine that manufactures ATP, the cell's energy currency, spinning like a turbine driven by a flow of protons. This structure captured the catalytic head of the motor and revealed how mechanical rotation is turned into chemical energy, earning a share of the 1997 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. It is one of nature's smallest and most elegant machines.
proteins.fun_fact: The central shaft of ATP synthase physically rotates, a genuine molecular motor spinning hundreds of times per second.

proteins.name: Prion Protein
proteins.tagline: The protein that can be infectious without any genes.
proteins.description: The prion protein is normally harmless on the surface of nerve cells, but it can flip into a misshapen form that forces other copies to misfold too, spreading like a molecular chain letter. These rogue proteins cause diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and 'mad cow' disease. Prions upended biology by showing that a protein alone can be infectious, with no DNA or RNA of its own.
proteins.fun_fact: Prion diseases are the only known infections caused by a protein with no genes, an idea that won the 1997 Nobel Prize in Medicine.

proteins.name: Streptavidin
proteins.tagline: Nature's molecular superglue.
proteins.description: Streptavidin clamps onto the small molecule biotin with one of the strongest non-covalent grips in all of biology. That near-unbreakable handshake makes the streptavidin-biotin pair an indispensable tool for sticking molecules together in labs and diagnostic tests. It is a four-part, barrel-shaped protein.
proteins.fun_fact: The streptavidin-biotin bond is so tight that it is routinely used as molecular 'superglue' in biotechnology.

proteins.name: Cu,Zn Superoxide Dismutase
proteins.tagline: A front-line defender against oxidative damage.
proteins.description: Superoxide dismutase neutralises harmful superoxide radicals, protecting cells from oxidative damage. It uses copper and zinc ions to rapidly convert the dangerous radical into ordinary oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. Mutations in the human version are linked to the motor-neuron disease ALS.
proteins.fun_fact: It works so fast that its speed is limited mainly by how quickly its targets can bump into it.

proteins.name: Calmodulin
proteins.tagline: The cell's universal calcium sensor.
proteins.description: Calmodulin is a small, dumbbell-shaped sensor that detects calcium ions, a universal cellular signal, and relays the message to dozens of partner proteins. When calcium rises, calmodulin wraps around and switches on its partners, influencing everything from muscle to memory. It is one of the cell's most versatile signalling hubs.
proteins.fun_fact: Calmodulin is so central to life that its sequence is almost unchanged across animals, plants and fungi.

proteins.name: Human Serum Albumin
proteins.tagline: The multipurpose delivery truck of your blood.
proteins.description: Serum albumin is the most abundant protein in blood plasma, acting as a delivery vehicle that carries fatty acids, hormones, metal ions and many drugs. It also helps keep fluid from leaking out of blood vessels by maintaining osmotic pressure. Because it binds so many medicines, it strongly influences how drugs travel through the body.
proteins.fun_fact: Albumin's fondness for binding drugs means doctors must account for it when calculating the right dose of many medicines.

proteins.name: DNA Polymerase I (Klenow Fragment)
proteins.tagline: The machine that copies your genome.
proteins.description: DNA polymerases copy DNA, adding one building block at a time to duplicate the genetic code before a cell divides. The Klenow fragment, a piece of the bacterial enzyme, was an early star of molecular biology and DNA sequencing. Its structure revealed a hand-like shape that grips DNA between 'fingers', 'palm' and 'thumb'.
proteins.fun_fact: Molecular biologists describe DNA polymerase as a right hand, with fingers, palm and thumb that close around the DNA.

proteins.name: SARS-CoV-2 Spike Glycoprotein
proteins.tagline: The protein at the heart of the COVID-19 vaccines.
proteins.description: The spike glycoprotein is the crown-like protein that studs the surface of the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus and lets it latch onto and enter human cells. Structures of the spike, solved within weeks of the virus's emergence, guided the design of the COVID-19 vaccines. Most of those vaccines teach the immune system to recognise exactly this protein.
proteins.fun_fact: This spike was solved and shared barely a month after the virus's genome was published, so vaccine design could begin almost immediately.
